name: Syria
sources: GDP $12.31bn and population 12.58m: World Bank WDI, NY.GDP.MKTP.CD and SP.POP.TOTL, Syrian Arab Republic, 1990.

The dollar GDP is an artefact of Syria's multiple official exchange rates. In 1990 the state ran an official rate near 11.2 pounds to the dollar, a separate 'neighbouring country' rate near 42, and a parallel market beyond that; the WDI conversion uses the official series, so this figure understates output against any purchasing-power measure. It is entered because it is the transcribed World Bank number and because Yemen, Jordan and Lebanon in this roster are converted the same way.
Inflation 19.4%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, 1990. The GDP deflator prints 23.8% the same year.

Interest rate 9.0% is administered, not a market rate. The World Bank publishes no lending-rate series for Syria in any year; the Commercial Bank of Syria set deposit and lending rates by decree in a banking system that was entirely state-owned until 2001. Recorded as an estimate.

Defence 6.9% of GDP: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS, 1990. The true burden was higher: Syrian procurement was financed by Soviet credits that never appeared in the budget, which is also why the debt figure below is what it is.

Debt 135% of GDP is an estimate. Syria stopped reporting to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System, so DT.DOD.DECT has no 1990 value; the standing estimate of Syrian external obligations around 1990 is roughly $16-17bn, the bulk of it military debt to the Soviet Union, against a $12.31bn GDP. That debt was written down by about 73% in the 2005 Russian settlement, which is the clearest evidence of its size.

Investment: World Bank NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS puts gross fixed capital formation at 16.5% of GDP in 1990, split here 11.0 public and 5.5 private, because the public sector held the commanding heights until the 1991 Investment Law No. 10.

Oil 0.379 mbd: Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy via Our World in Data, 1990 (235.2 TWh), converted at 620.5 TWh per million barrels a day. The same conversion reproduces the Saudi 6.4 and Egyptian 0.87 figures already in this roster.
System is Command: the Ba'athist public sector still held banking, insurance, foreign trade and heavy industry in January 1990. Authoritarianism 0.93 is Hafez al-Assad's Syria eight years after Hama.
Separatism 0.10 is the Kurdish northeast, where roughly 300,000 people had been stripped of citizenship by the 1962 Hasakah census and remained stateless.

Military index 18 sits between Egypt (14) and Iraq (26): roughly 400,000 men and 4,000 Soviet tanks, a force large enough to hold the Golan front and garrison Lebanon but decisively outclassed in the air since the Bekaa Valley in 1982.
